sought, which require outstanding achievements of their members, as judged by recognized
national or international experts in their disciplines or fields. 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(2}.
The Petitioner relies on the Beneficiary's membership in the Football Association (FA) as a licensed
coach and the National Soccer Coaches Association of America (NSCAA). On appeal, it
characterizes these associations as "distinguished" and the licensing process for FA as "rigorous."
At issue are the requirements to become a member of these organizations.
The Petitioner has not documented that either association requires the level of achievement specified
in the regulation. The record contains several FA certificates confirming the Beneficiary's
completion of modules, courses, and programs. The promotional materials about the FA affirm that
it is "leading the way in supporting and developing coaches, providing professional recognition at
every level." Membership is free and allows for reduced costs for national courses and access to FA
online courses. According to the Wikipedia entry the Petitioner supplied, the FA is the governing
body of association football in England, overseeing all of the country's professional football teams

and Olympic teams. 1 This information does not relate to the issue of FA's membership
requirements. According to the information on NSCAA's website, which the Petitioner submitted,
members enjoy discounts and access to group health insurance rates.
None of the above materials address how members are admitted to either association. While
licensure requires the successful completion of certain courses, the Petitioner has not shown that
passing a course constitutes an outstanding achievement. Moreover, certifications and licensure are
distinct from memberships: For example, in the immigrant visa context, the criteria for exceptional
ability include separate ones for licenses and certifications, and memberships. Compare 8 C.F.R.
§ 204.5(k)(3)(ii)(C) with (E). The record, therefore, does not confirm that either association requires
outstanding achievements of its members as judged by recognized national or international experts.

Moreover, information about the parent company does not demonstrate that is itself a
professional or major trade publication or major media. Finally, while we acknowledge that certain
blogs and other postings can reach the level of major media, the Petitioner has not corroborated the
reach and viewership of postings by " Thus, for all of these reasons, the Petitioner has
not established that the reports on constitute published material in qualifying publications
or major media.

The evidence does not support the contention that the Beneficiary has participated on a panel, or

In addition, he serves as president of the and his letter describes the

Mr. praises the coaching staff that the Beneficiary built. He does not, however, indicate that

Evidence of the alien's original scientific, scholarly, or business-related contributions of major
significance in the field. 8 C.F.R. § 214.2(o)(3)(iii)(B)(5).
Initially, the Petitioner relied on the success of players the Beneficiary has coached, as explained in
an unsigned letter from head coach of the men's soccer team at
The letter confirms that the university recruited players the Beneficiary coached at the
. Subsequently, the Petitioner offered its academy technical guide, which it
characterized as "publication of a curriculum designed to train ... fellow youth soccer coaches."
The Petitioner also provided letters from athletes affirming the Beneficiary's contributions to their
success. On appeal, it argues that the Beneficiary's curricula and influence on the success of those
he has coached are sufficient to meet this criterion.
The Beneficiary's curricula and coaching of players who have gone on to success do not qualify
under this criterion. First, the academic technical guide bears no indicia of publication and does not
list an author or otherwise credit the Beneficiary. The record also lacks evidence verifying that it has
been adopted beyond the Petitioner's organization. Accordingly, the Petitioner has not shown that it
constitutes a contribution of major significance in the field. Finally, the fact that players coached by
the Beneficiary have gone on to be recruited by colleges might confirm his influence on individual
athletes, but it is insufficient to demonstrate his impact in the field at a level consistent with a
contribution of major significance. Thus, the Petitioner has not satisfied this criterion.
